title: Toilet Safety Frames and Raised Seats With Arms: How to Choose One and Set It Up
subtitle: A plain-English guide to the sturdy armrests and taller seats that can make sitting down and standing up at the toilet a little easier.
excerpt: If getting up from the toilet has become a struggle, a safety frame or raised seat with arms may help. Here is how they differ, what they cost, and what to check before you buy.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Most toilets sit fairly low to the floor. For many of us, that was never a problem until knees, hips or balance started to change. Lowering down slowly and pushing back up can turn into a small daily struggle.

A toilet safety frame or a raised toilet seat with arms gives you two things: something solid to push against, and less distance to lower yourself. The Mayo Clinic Store's bathroom guide says a comfort-height toilet, raised seat or frame can reduce how far a person has to lower. It suggests these aids when wall-mounted bars are not possible.
"These can be useful in rental homes or bathrooms without proper wall blocking." (Mayo Clinic Store, guide to preventing falls in the bathroom)
How they work, and the main options

There are three common styles. A toilet safety frame that attaches to the toilet sits around it and gives you cushioned hand grips to push on. The Carex model below attaches directly to the toilet and adjusts to fit most toilets.

A stand-alone safety frame stands on its own around the toilet, with no installation. The Carex stand-alone model is about 30 inches wide, so it takes up more floor space than a frame that attaches to the toilet.

A raised toilet seat with arms adds a few inches of height and puts handles at your sides. The Drive model from Carewell lets you keep your existing seat and lid. The Drive model from Adaptive Specialties is described as a molded plastic seat with metal arms. Fit depends on your toilet's shape: the Carewell model is made for elongated bowls only, and Drive lists a separate model for standard bowls.

One honest limit: none of these prevents falls. They make sitting and standing easier, but one retailer's listing says a raised seat cannot support full body weight as you stand or sit. Where possible, combine a frame or raised seat with a wall-mounted grab bar. Your doctor, physical therapist or occupational therapist can help you choose the right aid, especially if you need help with transfers.

items: Toilet shape: fit depends on your toilet. Some raised seats fit elongated bowls only, so measure and read the product page before ordering.
Weight capacity: all four models below list 300 pounds. Check that it covers the person using it.
Height: a raised seat adds a set amount (3-1/2 inches or 5 inches for the two below), while the stand-alone frame adjusts from 24 to 29 inches. Ask your doctor or therapist what height suits you.
Floor space: the stand-alone frame is about 30 inches wide. Measure the gap between the toilet and nearby walls, tub or vanity.
Grips: cushioned grips are kinder to sore hands.
Returns: one seller below lists its item as non-returnable. Read each return policy before ordering.

Shipping: the Carex pages show a notice that orders may take more than 7 days to ship, and the Adaptive Specialties page lists the item as both in stock and backordered. Confirm timing before you buy.
Paying for it: Medicare does not cover fixtures like grab bars, so many buyers pay out of pocket. Carex lists FSA/HSA eligibility on its product pages; check with your plan.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well

Read the instructions all the way through first. Carex links a user guide on its stand-alone frame page, which is a good habit for any of these products. The Drive seat from Carewell attaches with screws, while the stand-alone frame needs no installation.

A wobbly frame or loose seat can become a hazard. After installing, check that the clamps and locks are secure, and check them again from time to time. Frames and arms also need a stable floor to sit on.

If you are buying for a parent, walk through the bathroom with them first. Note the toilet shape, the space on each side, and whether a grab bar could go on a nearby wall. The Mayo Clinic Store also advises doing a bathroom safety check before buying.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A sturdy frame or a few extra inches of height can make one of the most frequent trips of the day feel less tiring. Measure carefully, pick the style that fits your bathroom, and check with your doctor or therapist if you are unsure. Small steps like this add up.
